wordings.text: Which of these grows fastest as n becomes large?

questions.explanation:
Any exponential eventually overtakes any polynomial: at n = 20, 2ⁿ is about a million and
n³ is 8,000. Among the others, n³ > n² log n > n log n.

wordings.text: What is 3n² + 100n + 5 in big O notation?

questions.explanation:
Big O keeps the fastest-growing term and drops constant factors: for large n, n² dominates
100n and 5. O(3n²) and O(n² + n) mean the same set but are not simplified.
questions.summary: Simplifying a polynomial in big O

wordings.text: A function loops once over an array a of length A, and after that once over an array b of length B. What is its runtime?

questions.explanation:
The loops run one after the other, so their costs add. They would multiply if the loop
over b ran inside the loop over a. With two independent inputs, keep both sizes.
questions.summary: Runtime of two loops over different inputs

wordings.text: Quicksort always takes the first element as its pivot. On which input is it slowest?
options: A list with all values different

questions.explanation:
On sorted input the first element is the smallest, so each split leaves n - 1 elements
on one side: O(n²). On random input the splits are balanced on average: O(n log n).
A random pivot makes the worst case unlikely for any input.
questions.summary: Worst case of quicksort with a fixed pivot

wordings.text: A hash map lookup is called O(1). Which case does that describe?
options: The expected case, with a hash function that spreads keys well
The worst case for any keys
Every lookup, whatever the hash function

questions.explanation:
On average each slot holds few keys. In the worst case all keys collide and a lookup
scans O(n) of them; a good hash function makes that unlikely.
questions.summary: Which case the constant-time hash lookup refers to

wordings.text: sum(a, n) returns a[n - 1] + sum(a, n - 1), and 0 when n is 0. How much extra memory does sum(a, n) use?

questions.explanation:
Every call waits for the next one, so n frames are on the call stack at the deepest
point. A loop with one running total needs O(1).
questions.summary: Call stack memory of linear recursion

wordings.text: An array is reversed in place by swapping the first and last elements, then the second and second-to-last, and so on. How much extra memory does it use?

questions.explanation:
Only two indices and one value for the swap are stored, whatever the size of the array.
The input itself is not counted as extra memory.
questions.summary: Extra memory of an in-place reverse

questions.explanation:
The inner loop runs n - 1, n - 2, …, 0 times, n(n - 1)/2 in total. Halving the work of a
full n × n loop does not change the class.
questions.summary: Runtime of a loop over all pairs

wordings.text:
What is the runtime of this loop?

```
while n > 1:
    n = n / 2, rounded down
```

questions.explanation:
Halving reaches 1 after about log₂ n steps. Any loop that divides its range by a constant
factor each time is logarithmic, as in binary search.

wordings.text:
What is the runtime of this loop?

```
for i from 1 to n:
    j = 1
    while j < n:
        j = j * 2
```

questions.explanation:
The inner loop doubles j until it reaches n, about log₂ n steps, and does not depend on
i. It runs n times: O(n log n).
questions.summary: Runtime of a logarithmic loop inside a linear one

wordings.text: f(n) returns f(n - 1) + f(n - 1), and 1 when n is 0. What is the runtime of f(n)?

questions.explanation:
Each call makes two more, so level k of the call tree has 2ᵏ calls and there are n
levels. A rule of thumb: branches to the power of depth. Computing f(n - 1) once and
doubling it is O(n).
questions.summary: Runtime of a function with two recursive calls

wordings.text: Merge sort splits the input in half, sorts both halves recursively and merges them in linear time: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). What is T(n)?

questions.explanation:
Each of the log₂ n levels of halving does O(n) merging in total. Binary search, one half
with constant work, is T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) = O(log n).

wordings.text: A recursive function makes one call on an input of half the size and does constant work besides. What is its runtime?

questions.explanation:
T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1): there are about log₂ n calls, each doing constant work. Binary
search has this shape.
questions.summary: Runtime of recursion that halves its input

wordings.text: A dynamic array grows by a fixed 10 slots when it is full, copying all its elements. What do n appends cost in total?

questions.explanation:
A copy happens every 10 appends and copies all elements so far: 10 + 20 + 30 + … up to n,
about n²/20. Growing by a constant factor, such as doubling, keeps the total at O(n).
questions.summary: Why arrays grow by a factor and not a fixed amount

wordings.text: What does it mean that an operation costs O(1) amortized?
options: Any sequence of n operations costs O(n) in total, though a single one may cost more
It costs O(1) on average over random inputs
It costs O(1) with high probability

questions.explanation:
Amortized cost spreads the rare expensive operations, such as an array resize, over the
cheap ones. It is a guarantee for every sequence, unlike expected cost, which averages
over chance.

wordings.text: What does inserting a value into a sorted array of n elements cost, keeping it sorted?

questions.explanation:
Binary search finds the place in O(log n), but the elements after it must shift one place
each, O(n). A balanced search tree inserts in O(log n).
questions.summary: Cost of a sorted insert into an array

wordings.text: What does it cost to turn an unordered array of n values into a binary heap in place, by sifting down from the last parent to the root?

questions.explanation:
Most nodes are near the bottom and sift down only a little: half of them not at all, a
quarter one level, and so on, which sums to O(n). Pushing the n values one by one costs
O(n log n).
questions.summary: Cost of building a heap from an array

wordings.text: Which of these cost O(log n) for a structure of n elements?
options: Searching a balanced binary search tree
Adding a value to a binary heap
Looking up a key in a hash map, on average
Reading an array element by index
Adding a node at the head of a linked list

questions.explanation:
Both walk one path of a tree of height O(log n). A hash lookup on average, an array read
and a head insert are O(1).
